channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: After an explosives-laden drone was found at Leipzig's air-freight hub and drones were sighted over military sites, Chancellor Merz convened Germany's National Security Council, blaming Russian "hybrid warfare" and pledging to expand drone defences.
item.description:
A string of drone incidents has put Germany on high security alert. After a drone carrying explosives was discovered at the Leipzig/Halle airport — a major air-freight hub — on 5 August, and further drones were sighted over Bundeswehr military sites, Chancellor Friedrich Merz convened the National Security Council. Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt called the intrusions a possible act by "foreign powers," and Berlin pointed to Russian "hybrid warfare" — the use of sabotage, drones and other deniable tactics below the threshold of open war. The government plans to expand drone defences, including a new research centre at the German Aerospace Center in Saxony-Anhalt and letting companies defend their own sites, though the coalition is split over a tangle of 40 different responsible authorities. The episode fed a wider debate about defence priorities: Moritz Schularick, head of the Kiel Institute for the World Economy, argued that Germany is misspending the up to EUR 700 billion earmarked for the military through 2030 on tanks and frigates instead of the AI, robotics, drones and satellite technology that modern conflict demands, and called for a central procurement coordinator.

Industry Impact

Rising hybrid-warfare risk around German industrial and logistics infrastructure is a new operational and security consideration for manufacturers, including chemical sites and the freight hubs they depend on. Repeated drone disruption at airports and plants threatens supply-chain reliability and raises security costs. At the same time, Germany's vast defence-spending programme — if redirected toward advanced technology — represents a growing market for high-performance materials, including the specialty adhesives, coatings and sealants used in drones, satellites, sensors and electronics. For chemical suppliers, the dual message is to harden site and logistics security against hybrid threats while positioning for defence-linked demand in advanced-manufacturing applications.

Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung | Frankfurter Rundschau | Chinatimes | Süddeutsche Zeitung | Die Zeit

item.title: Chancellor Merz moved to shield carmakers from tougher EU plug-in-hybrid CO2 rules as German brands shift research and output abroad to survive, while South America's car markets split — Brazil's production booming as Argentina's registrations slump 30%.
item.description:
Pressures on the global car industry — a major consumer of adhesives, coatings and sealants — pulled in different directions. In Germany, Chancellor Friedrich Merz moved to stop the European Commission from further tightening how plug-in hybrids and range-extender vehicles (which pair a small combustion engine with an electric drivetrain) count toward manufacturers' fleet CO2 targets. The scheduled January 2027 downgrade would credit hybrids less, forcing carmakers to sell many more pure electric cars — often at a discount — to stay within limits. Separately, a leading auto economist warned that VW, BMW and Mercedes are cutting models and jobs and relocating research and production abroad, especially "in China, for China," because they cannot match Chinese rivals on the technology and cost of digital, electric cars while home sales slide. In South America the picture diverged sharply: Brazil's vehicle output rose 8.8% in the first half — the world's second-fastest growth after India — with July sales the best of the year, even as Argentina's registrations plunged 30.3% year-on-year in July under a harsh economic adjustment.

Industry Impact

Automotive is one of the largest markets for adhesives, coatings and sealants, and each shift moves demand. The EU CO2 fight will shape the powertrain mix — more electric vehicles means more structural bonding, battery sealing and thermal-management chemistry, but a forced, loss-making EV push could also shrink German output and pricing power. German carmakers relocating to China move ACS demand with them, favouring suppliers with a strong Asian footprint. And the Brazil-Argentina split shows why regional balance matters: booming Brazilian production is a bright spot for automotive chemistry even as Argentina contracts. Suppliers should align capacity and development with where vehicles are actually being built — increasingly Asia and Brazil rather than a shrinking German base.

WirtschaftsWoche | Neue Zürcher Zeitung | Valor Econômico | China Economic Net | La Nación

item.title: Indonesia said it is open to a preferential trade deal with the South American bloc Mercosur, using Brazil as a gateway, and urged fellow BRICS nations to deepen cooperation as the rules-based global trading system fragments.
item.description:
Indonesia signalled a push to diversify its trade partnerships as US-led protectionism reshapes global commerce. On the sidelines of the BRICS trade ministers' meeting in Jaipur, India, on 7 August, Indonesian Trade Minister Budi Santoso said Jakarta is open to a preferential trade agreement (a pact that lowers, though does not eliminate, tariffs between members) with Mercosur — the South American customs union of Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay — using Brazil as the entry point. Two-way Indonesia-Brazil trade reached USD 3.53 billion in the first half of 2026 and USD 7 billion in 2025; Indonesia's main exports to Brazil include animal and vegetable fats, vehicles and parts, electrical machinery and rubber products. Santoso also urged BRICS members — the bloc of major emerging economies now including Indonesia — to deepen cooperation, warning that the rules-based trading system is eroding and the global economy is fragmenting. The moves illustrate how mid-sized economies are hedging against US tariffs and a weakening World Trade Organization by weaving new South-South links among emerging markets.

Industry Impact

A gradual re-wiring of trade toward emerging-market blocs is reshaping where chemical demand grows and how goods move. New South-South agreements like an Indonesia-Mercosur deal could open faster-growing markets for manufactured goods — and the adhesives, coatings and sealants embedded in them — while shifting competitive dynamics away from traditional US and European channels. For chemical producers, the strategic signal is that ASEAN and Latin America are deepening direct ties that bypass Western hubs, rewarding suppliers with local presence and flexible regional supply chains. It also underlines the broader fragmentation theme: as global rules weaken, a patchwork of bilateral and bloc deals will increasingly determine market access and tariff exposure.

Antara News | Kompas | Antara News

item.title: Washington opened new tariff fronts, imposing 10–12.5% duties on goods from 60 trading partners over forced-labour concerns, threatening Switzerland over its trade surplus, and setting a polysilicon tariff that quietly benefits Germany's Wacker Chemie.
item.description:
The US widened its tariff campaign on several fronts. The Office of the US Trade Representative imposed new duties of 10–12.5% on goods from 60 trading partners in late July, invoking Section 301 of the 1974 Trade Act — a tool that lets Washington retaliate against foreign practices it deems unfair — this time citing the partners' alleged failure to ban imports made with forced labour. The duties bite hardest on developing exporters; about 55% of India's exports to the US fall within scope, though generic pharmaceuticals and smartphones are exempt. Separately, President Trump publicly threatened Switzerland, claiming a USD 39 billion US trade deficit with the country and boasting he could "wipe out" it in one stroke — a fresh broadside at a European economy, triggered partly by his irritation at low Swiss interest rates. And in the chemical arena, Swiss daily NZZ highlighted that Trump's new 15% tariff plus minimum import prices on polysilicon (USD 21 per kilogram of raw material, far above spot) — nominally aimed at China — hands a windfall to Germany's Wacker Chemie, a leading Western polysilicon maker, while giving foreign producers 120 days to relocate to the US.

Industry Impact

The proliferation of overlapping US tariffs — by country, by product and by policy pretext — is a defining risk for globally sourced chemical supply chains. Broad Section 301 duties on 60 countries raise landed costs on a vast range of manufactured inputs and finished goods, while ad hoc threats against partners like Switzerland show no European economy is off-limits. The polysilicon case is a reminder that tariffs create winners as well as losers: a well-placed Western chemical producer can gain protected pricing and reshoring demand. For adhesives, coatings and sealants suppliers, the takeaways are to map tariff exposure across the full supplier chain, watch for both cost hits and protected-market opportunities, and expect further retaliation and copy-cat measures.

China Daily | Neue Zürcher Zeitung | Neue Zürcher Zeitung

item.title: China's imports jumped 27.5% and exports rose 23.9% in July from a year earlier, a striking acceleration, as Beijing's leadership and central bank signalled fresh stimulus including likely cuts to interest rates and bank reserve requirements.
item.description:
China's external trade accelerated sharply in July: imports surged 27.5% and exports rose 23.9% from a year earlier, according to customs data, with exports of computers and related parts up 45.2% in the first seven months. Growth was broad-based across partners — July exports to ASEAN rose 38.4% and to Africa 18.2%, while imports from Russia, ASEAN and the US also jumped — underscoring China's industrial momentum despite US tariffs and tech restrictions. At the same time, Beijing is preparing to support demand at home. A late-July meeting of the Communist Party's Politburo, chaired by President Xi Jinping, prioritised "effective expansion of domestic demand" and lifting services consumption; China's services retail sales grew 5.3% in the first half, outpacing goods by 4.2 points. The People's Bank of China then signalled it has "sufficient" policy tools and will roll out incremental measures; analysts expect cuts to the reserve requirement ratio (the share of deposits banks must park at the central bank, so lowering it frees up money to lend), interest-rate cuts and stronger targeted credit. The combination — export strength plus looming stimulus — sets China apart from a stagnating Europe.

Industry Impact

China is both the biggest competitive threat and, potentially, the best near-term demand story for chemical producers this year. Surging trade and planned stimulus point to resilient Chinese industrial and construction activity — supportive of demand for adhesives, coatings and sealants in electronics, autos, packaging and building — even as the same export machine pressures European rivals (see other insight in this alert). Rate and reserve cuts would further lift construction and consumption, the core ACS end-markets. Suppliers with a strong China position may find growth there that Europe cannot offer, but should weigh overcapacity, local competition and policy risk. Tracking the timing and size of Beijing's easing is key to sizing second-half Chinese demand.

Hürriyet Daily News | China Economic Net | China Economic Net

item.title: German exports hit a record EUR 139.3 billion in June even as output barely grew, yet the trade deficit with China widened to about EUR 55 billion as German exports there slumped over 12%, dropping China to Germany's ninth-largest goods market.
item.description:
Germany's industrial data painted a picture of an export machine still humming abroad while losing ground in a key market. Industrial production rose a modest 0.2% in June, lifted by a 3.6% gain in autos and 8.4% in other transport equipment but dragged by a 3.9% fall in machinery, according to the federal statistics office Destatis. Exports climbed 0.9% on the month to a record EUR 139.3 billion, up 6.6% on a year earlier. Yet the China relationship is deteriorating: in the first half, German exports to China fell more than 12% to just under EUR 37 billion — pushing China down to only Germany's ninth-largest goods market — while German imports from China rose 8.9% to EUR 91.8 billion, widening the bilateral deficit from EUR 40 billion a year earlier to roughly EUR 55 billion. China nonetheless remains Germany's single biggest overall trading partner, just ahead of the US. Economists tie the export slide to a structural shift: Chinese firms increasingly make at home what they once imported, and Chinese overcapacity in electric cars, batteries, machinery and solar modules is flooding into Europe at prices local producers struggle to match.

Industry Impact

The data capture a strategic squeeze on the German industrial base that anchors European demand for adhesives, coatings and sealants: still competitive globally, but steadily displaced in and by China. As Chinese customers substitute domestic supply and Chinese exporters undercut European rivals at home, the German manufacturers that buy ACS products face thinner margins and volume pressure — bad for regional demand. The record headline export figure masks this erosion. For chemical suppliers, the implication is to follow customers into growth markets and higher-value applications rather than rely on a maturing German-China trade axis, and to watch Chinese overcapacity as a direct competitive threat in European coatings, battery and automotive chemistries.

MarketScreener | Handelsblatt | MarketScreener | Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung

item.title: The US unexpectedly shed 23,000 jobs in July, its first decline since February, and prior months were revised sharply lower, pushing markets to bet the Federal Reserve will wait until December before raising interest rates.
item.description:
The US labour market weakened abruptly in July, with employers cutting 23,000 jobs — the first monthly decline since February — against expectations of solid gains, according to the Labor Department. Adding to the gloom, payrolls for May and June were revised down by a combined 103,000. The unemployment rate slipped to 4.1%, but for the wrong reason: people left the workforce rather than found jobs. The losses were led by local education (-50,000), retail and warehousing (-19,000) and financial firms (-14,000), while health care kept adding jobs, if more slowly. The soft data reshaped interest-rate expectations. Only days earlier several Federal Reserve officials had floated a September rate hike to fight sticky inflation (a running theme in prior alerts); now markets have sharply cut the odds of a September or October move and price roughly an 85% chance that any hike waits until December, with Minneapolis Fed chief Neel Kashkari favouring gradual increases. Fed officials remain frustrated that inflation has run above their 2% target for five years, blaming war-driven energy prices and tariffs — leaving them caught between a cooling jobs market and stubborn prices.

Industry Impact

The rate path set in Washington ripples worldwide through the dollar and the cost of capital. A Fed that holds off until December keeps financing conditions looser for longer, modestly supporting the rate-sensitive construction and manufacturing demand that drives adhesives, coatings and sealants — and a softer dollar would ease raw-material bills for European and Asian buyers. But a cooling US jobs market also signals weakening end-demand in the world's largest economy, a caution for suppliers to US housing and industry. Encouragingly, US construction employment still rose by 22,000 in July, suggesting building activity — a core ACS end-market — is holding up better than the headline. Treasurers should keep flexibility for a later-than-feared, but still possible, US rate rise.

Axios | Dünya Gazetesi | The New York Times | Associated Builders and Contractors

item.title: A heatwave and drought sent European power prices surging — forcing nuclear shutdowns from Hungary to France — while parched fields threaten French and German harvests and a typhoon disrupted China's busiest port.
item.description:
Extreme heat and drought are simultaneously straining Europe's energy, farming and freight systems. Day-ahead electricity prices surged as cooling demand spiked and low rivers throttled generation: Hungary fully shut its Paks nuclear plant on Monday — the first time in 44 years — after record-low Danube levels cut cooling water; Romania idled one of two reactors at Cernavoda; and France's EDF halted three reactors at the Chooz and Cattenom plants as the Meuse and Moselle rivers ran low. The Rhine, which carries roughly 80% of Germany's inland-waterway freight (about 285 million tonnes a year), is again too shallow for full barge loads, pushing up transport costs. Agriculture is being hit hard: France's largest farm union, the FNSEA, is demanding a multi-billion-euro emergency plan as corn harvests are seen falling around 35% — the worst since 1980 — and rapeseed sowing is at risk; the government has promised a "global plan." German regions such as Baden-Württemberg report falling yields, spreading pests and an expected one-third drop in sugar output. The disruption is not only European: Typhoon White Dolphin, the year's thirteenth, struck China's east coast, suspending some container operations at Ningbo-Zhoushan, the world's busiest cargo port.

Industry Impact

Weather is now a recurring cost and supply shock across the chemical value chain. Higher power prices and constrained Rhine barge logistics hit German chemical production economics directly — energy and freight are major cost lines — and can force output curbs at riverside plants. Crop failures raise the cost of bio-based and agricultural feedstocks and dampen rural demand for construction and equipment. Port disruption in China, meanwhile, threatens short-term delays to goods and chemical shipments through a key global gateway. The pattern argues for climate resilience in operations and sourcing: diversified logistics beyond low rivers, energy-cost hedging, and contingency stock ahead of the now-annual summer drought and typhoon seasons.

Anadolu Agency | Daily Sabah | Le Parisien | Le Dauphiné Libéré | Tagesschau | Lianhe Zaobao

item.title: President Trump convened global mining executives and pledged about USD 3 billion in loans to secure critical minerals such as rare earths, tungsten and scandium for defence and to cut US dependence on China.
item.description:
President Trump gathered executives from some of the world's largest mining companies at the State Department on 7 August as his administration intensified a drive to lock in domestic and allied supplies of critical minerals — the metals essential to weapons, electronics and clean energy. The White House says it needs rare earths, tungsten, germanium and scandium to replenish weapons stockpiles drained during the Iran conflict and to reduce reliance on China, which dominates supply. Alongside the summit, Trump announced roughly USD 3 billion in federal loans: USD 1.4 billion to battery-materials maker Sila Nanotechnologies, USD 400 million to Sunrise Energy Metals' Syerston scandium project in Australia (with the US Department of War taking first rights to its output), USD 150 million to magnet developer Niron Magnetics, plus smaller export-import loans to other miners. Scandium — a lightweight metal used in aerospace alloys and fuel cells — is telling: the US has not mined it since 1969, and nearly all supply comes from China, Russia and Ukraine. Analysts caution, though, that the deeper bottleneck is not tungsten deposits but the scarcity of new discoveries and advanced projects, which take years to develop against fast-rising demand.

Industry Impact

The reshoring of critical-mineral supply chains is remapping raw-material availability and pricing well beyond metals, and the logic increasingly overrides lowest-cost sourcing for anything deemed strategic. For chemical producers, the near-term read-through is more state intervention in feedstock markets, potential retaliation from China (which has already tightened rare-earth and related export controls in prior alerts), and a premium on securing and dual-sourcing specialty inputs. Companies exposed to electronics-grade materials, catalysts or metal-bearing additives should map their dependence on Chinese-controlled minerals and factor multi-year supply risk into procurement. The direction is clear: "critical" designations are spreading, and buffer stocks plus qualified alternative suppliers are becoming competitive necessities.

The Straits Times | Lianhe Zaobao | ABC | Wallstreet-Online | The Economic Times

item.title: The US Senate passed the Graham Act, authorising President Trump to impose tariffs up to 500% on Russian goods and up to 100% on major buyers of Russian oil and gas — India, China and Turkey — pending a House vote in September.
item.description:
The US Senate approved the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 — a bill named after the late Republican senator — that hands President Trump sweeping new economic weapons against Moscow and its energy customers. It authorises tariffs of up to 500% on Russian imports, including oil and natural gas, and up to 100% on countries that buy large volumes of Russian oil or gas, explicitly naming the top buyers India, China and Turkey. The act also targets Russian banks, officials, President Putin's inner circle, oligarchs and the "shadow fleet" of tankers used to evade existing oil-export limits. Senate passage is only the first step: the House of Representatives is on summer recess and will not vote before early September, and the tariffs are permissive — Trump "may," not "must," impose them — leaving room for negotiation. Still, the vote signals bipartisan appetite to squeeze Russia's war revenues through secondary sanctions that would, for the first time, penalise third countries for their energy trade with Moscow.

Industry Impact

Secondary tariffs on India and China — two of the fastest-growing chemical markets and major manufacturing hubs — could sharply reroute global trade flows and raise costs across supply chains that touch adhesives, coatings and sealants. A 100% US tariff on goods from those countries would ripple far beyond energy, hitting intermediates, packaging and finished goods, and could invite retaliation. Even the threat injects fresh uncertainty into sourcing decisions and Asian demand. Chemical producers with Indian or Chinese operations or suppliers should scenario-plan for tariff exposure and possible supply reshoring, while watching the September House vote as the trigger that turns a permissive authority into real duties.

The Times of India | Commercial Times | LiveMint

item.title: The EU's Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation is now in force and a ban on PFAS "forever chemicals" in paper food packaging starts on 12 August, forcing reformulation across the packaging and coatings chain.
item.description:
The European Union's Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR) — a sweeping law governing packaging from design to disposal — took effect in August 2026. It requires all packaging placed on the EU market to be recyclable, sets graded recyclability targets (at least 95%, 80% or 70% by 2030 depending on grade), phases out many single-use plastics from 2030, and makes producers pay recycling fees under "extended producer responsibility" (the principle that the maker funds end-of-life handling). Crucially for chemistry, from 12 August 2026 the EU bans PFAS — per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, the water- and grease-repellent "forever chemicals" prized for durability but linked to health concerns — in paper boxes, trays and food wrapping, forcing food and packaging firms to strip out PFAS coatings and file conformity paperwork. The rules reach well beyond Europe, hitting exporters in textiles, electronics, steel and packaging across Asia. Separately, Drägerwerk's chief executive publicly urged Berlin to resist a far broader EU-wide PFAS restriction now under debate, warning it would endanger Germany as an industrial base — a sign of mounting industry pushback.

Industry Impact

This lands squarely in Henkel's core Adhesives, Coatings & Sealants (ACS) markets. The PFAS paper-packaging ban and the PPWR's design-for-recycling rules directly reshape demand for functional coatings, barrier layers and adhesives: PFAS-based grease and water barriers must be replaced with compliant alternatives, and adhesives must not compromise a package's recyclability grade. That is both a compliance burden and a growth opening for suppliers with PFAS-free, recyclable-compatible chemistries ready to qualify. The looming broader PFAS restriction is a strategic risk across many formulations and warrants active regulatory tracking and reformulation roadmaps now. Firms that lead on compliant chemistry can win share as converters scramble to meet the 12 August deadline and the 2030 recyclability thresholds.

Vietnam Investment Review | TuoiTreNews | Yahoo Germany

item.title: Germany's main industry association, the BDI, expects the Iran war to shave nearly half a point off global growth to about 3% and lift world inflation above 4.5%, as the IMF cuts its euro-zone forecast to 0.9%.
item.description:
The Federation of German Industries (BDI) — the umbrella body for German industry — said the Iran war is materially dragging on the world economy. It expects global growth to slow by almost half a percentage point to 3% this year; without the war, recovering demand and the artificial-intelligence investment boom would have lifted growth toward 3.3%–3.4% (2025: 3.2%). The BDI sees global inflation climbing by more than a percentage point to above 4.5% as war-driven energy costs feed through. For Germany itself, it forecasts real growth of just 0.6%, despite a surprisingly solid second quarter. The gloom is echoed by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), which has cut its 2026 euro-area growth forecast for the second time in a quarter, to 0.9% from 1.1%, and trimmed its global projection to 3.0%, while leaving 2027 euro-zone growth at 1.2%. Both institutions frame the downgrade as a war-and-tariffs story: higher oil prices, disrupted trade routes and US import duties are simultaneously slowing activity and keeping prices high — an uncomfortable mix of weak growth and sticky inflation.

Industry Impact

Sub-1% growth in the euro zone and Germany points to another lean year for the construction and manufacturing customers that buy most adhesives, coatings and sealants, with little organic volume growth to count on. Persistently high inflation keeps raw-material and wage costs elevated and limits how far central banks can cut rates to revive demand — the stagflation-lite backdrop that squeezes chemical margins from both ends. Planning should lean on defensive assumptions: flat-to-soft European volumes, cost discipline, and market-share gains rather than a demand rebound. Regions less exposed to the war's drag (see other insight in this alert on China's trade surge) may offer better growth than a stagnant Europe.

Handelsblatt | Süddeutsche Zeitung | China Economic Net

item.title: Iran's Revolutionary Guards insist the Strait of Hormuz will stay closed until Washington ends the war, lifts its blockade of Iranian ports and pays compensation, hardening a standoff that keeps global oil and chemical supply chains on edge.
item.description:
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps — the elite military branch that polices the Gulf — said the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow lane that normally carries about a fifth of the world's oil, will remain closed until the United States meets "all" of Tehran's conditions: definitively ending the war against Iran and its allies, lifting the blockade on Iranian ports, fully compensating Iran for war damage, removing sanctions and unfreezing Iranian assets. Reopening the strait is now President Trump's stated top priority, but the maximalist terms point to a prolonged deadlock. As of 9 August, US Central Command had redirected at least 55 vessels to enforce its own blockade of Iranian ports. Markets read the diplomatic flurry as tentatively hopeful: Brent crude ended the week around USD 83.55 a barrel, still down more than 8%. Resource-poor Japan, which ships over 90% of its crude through Hormuz, is designing a scheme to share the extra cost of rerouting tankers around the strait. Analysts warn that even once fighting stops, Gulf shipping and regional chemical supply chains could take months to normalise.

Industry Impact

For the Adhesives, Coatings & Sealants (ACS) industry, a prolonged Hormuz closure means sustained volatility in the oil and petrochemical feedstocks that underpin resins, solvents and polymers, plus higher and less predictable freight and insurance costs on any Gulf-linked cargo. The chemical trade press notes that industry forecasters had assumed the conflict would be resolved by mid-year — an assumption that has failed, leaving pricing models built on stale premises. Producers should assume elevated input-cost risk into the fourth quarter, keep buffer stocks of critical feedstocks, and build price-escalation clauses into contracts. The wider signal is that energy-linked cost shocks, not weak demand, remain the dominant swing factor for chemical margins this year.

La Presse | LiveMint | Kompas | The Mainichi | Adhesives & Sealants Industry
